_internal: `role` names the part a need plays in the economy (hunger: the need whose unmet floor counts as hunger; fuel: the need a hearth's cooking fuel is added to; household_work: the need met by hours of household work), read through sim/economy/need_roles.py. `subsistence_from_climate` names the floor per person sim/world/climate_needs.py calculates for each tile from its climate. TRANSITIONAL: surplus_budget_share is a labelled heuristic weight per need (water's is small because its floor is most of what a household spends on it) (normalised over the needs that have a priced good). A good's effectiveness is per unit of its own production unit, in the need's unit. Mods add needs (ids namespaced by mod id) and add or extend goods; a production entry may also carry `satisfies` for its dominant output.

food.effectiveness_basis: food energy per kg relative to wheat grain
food.satiation_basis: BIOLOGICAL limit, not a heuristic: well-fed modern intake, about 3,300 kcal per person per day (FAO food balance sheets: dietary energy supply in 2021 was about 3,460 kcal a head a day in Europe and 3,880 in Northern America, FAO food balance sheets update, https://www.fao.org/3/cc8088en/cc8088en.pdf; supply includes household waste, so intake is lower), over the 3,400 kcal per kg of wheat the subsistence figure uses, a year of it: 1.5 times the subsistence quantity. Food beyond it is stored, sold, fed to animals or wasted. Held equal to sim/world/agriculture.py MAXIMUM_INTAKE_MULTIPLE_OF_SUBSISTENCE by a test.

shelter.satiation_basis: Past a roomy dwelling, more wall and roof is not wanted, and a household that has money left builds no more house with it. The floor is the Sphere minimum covered area of 3.5 square metres a head; living space in pre-industrial housing was of the order of ten square metres a head, 2.857 times that: Naroll, Floor Area and Settlement Population, American Antiquity 27(4) 1962, abstract (opened), population 'very roughly estimated as of the order of one-tenth the floor area in square meters', so about 10 square metres a head, and 10 / 3.5 = 2.857; Brown, Cross-Cultural Research 21 (1987), via the HRAF summary (opened), a constant of 6 square metres a head from a 38 culture sample, which is a mean occupancy and so a lower bound on a roomy dwelling, not the limit. Both are cross-cultural means of settlement dwellings, not a measured limit of wanting more room: confidence D, a labelled heuristic, Complaints/646. A further data point, Wikipedia, Insula (building) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insula_(building), opened, tagged citation needed): a typical Roman insula held over 40 people in 3,600 square feet (330 square metres), 8.25 square metres a head, which is again an occupancy and so a lower bound. The limit is that multiple of the tile's own floor, since the floor follows the climate's wall thickness.
shelter.unit: cubic metres of wall or frame
shelter.effectiveness_basis: volume of structure one unit builds

clothing.effectiveness_basis: cover and warmth per kg relative to plain woven cloth

implements_and_arms.effectiveness_basis: working hardness and edge holding per kg relative to bronze

health.effectiveness_basis: relative therapeutic or hygienic effect per kg

ornament.unit: kg of bright durable metal equivalent
ornament.satiation_basis: Ornament metal is durable, so yearly purchase is wear and loss of the stock held, not the budget share: stock held times the loss rate. Stock held, about 25 g a head: all gold ever mined, 201,296 tonnes above ground in 2020 (Wikipedia, Gold, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold, opened), over a world population of 7.84 billion in 2020 (Wikipedia, World population, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_population, opened) is 25.7 g a head, a modern upper bound for a pre-industrial stock. Loss rate, about 1 per cent a year: service_lives.json gold_kg (a forum estimate of coin loss, 1 / 100 years; ring wear alone about 6 mg a year). 25 g x 0.01 = 0.25 g = 0.00025 kg a head a year (was 0.0005 from an unsourced 2 per cent). Confidence C. Validation bound used by tests: at most a few grams per head per year.
ornament.effectiveness_basis: display value per kg of worked metal; a cultural quantity, equal across the bright metals

seasoning.satiation_basis: TRANSITIONAL heuristic: spices are bought for taste and to dress plain food, and a household's yearly use is grams, not a budget share; a couple of grams per head a year is an order of magnitude, not a measured figure. A model of taste, and of how far an elite's use exceeds the common people's, would replace it.
seasoning.effectiveness_basis: flavouring strength per kg relative to black pepper; taken equal across the spices until a source gives them separately

salt.subsistence_basis: BIOLOGICAL requirement: the Institute of Medicine Adequate Intake for adult sodium is 1.5 g a day (Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate, National Academies Press, 2005), set to cover sodium lost in sweat by people active in heat. Sodium is 39.3 per cent of sodium chloride by mass (22.99 / 58.44), so 1.5 g of sodium is 3.81 g of salt a day, 3.81 * 365 = 1.39 kg a year. Bare survival needs far less on a cool, idle day; this is the floor for working people in a warm climate. Source opened (National Academies Press, Dietary Reference Intakes for Water, Potassium, Sodium, Chloride, and Sulfate, 2005, Summary, nationalacademies.org/read/10925/chapter/2): 'The AI for sodium is set for young adults at 1.5 g (65 mmol)/day (3.8 g of sodium chloride)' 'to cover sodium sweat losses in unacclimatized individuals who are exposed to high temperatures'; confidence C.
salt.satiation_basis: BIOLOGICAL limit: the observed world mean salt intake, past which the extra only harms. Source opened (Powles et al., Global, regional and national sodium intakes in 1990 and 2010, BMJ Open 2013;3:e003733, doi:10.1136/bmjopen-2013-003733, abstract): 'In 2010, global mean sodium intake was 3.95 g/day (95% uncertainty interval: 3.89 to 4.01). This was nearly twice the WHO recommended limit of 2 g/day and equivalent to 10.06 (9.88-10.21) g/day of salt.' 10.06 * 365 = 3.67 kg a year (this is an intake people eat, taken as the level past which more is not wanted); confidence C.
salt.effectiveness_basis: mass of sodium chloride; rock, solar and brine salt are equal

water.subsistence_basis: 20 litres a head a day, the basic-access service level of Howard and Bartram, Domestic Water Quantity, Service Level and Health (WHO/SDE/WSH/03.02, 2003; opened): service level table, 'Basic access (average quantity unlikely to exceed 20 l/c/d)', with a basic minimum of 7.5 litres a head a day for drinking and food in hot conditions; enough for drinking, cooking and basic hygiene. One litre is one kilogram, so 20 * 365 = 7300 kg; confidence C.
water.satiation_basis: TRANSITIONAL heuristic: 100 litres a head a day, the 'optimal access' level of the same WHO report, past which more water is waste, not use. Roman fountains ran at far higher flows; that is a flow, not a use per head.
water.unit: kg of water at the point of use
water.effectiveness_basis: mass of water delivered; every way of delivering it is equal

vessels.stock_basis: A household holds a few dozen vessels (cooking pots, storage jars, bowls, cups) of about a kilogram each, about 5 kg a head, and they break and are replaced within a few years: cooking pots last the least, storage jars the most. Source opened (Ben A. Nelson, Ceramic Frequency and Use-Life: A Highland Mayan Case in Cross-Cultural Perspective, ch. 8 of W. A. Longacre ed., Ceramic Ethnoarchaeology, University of Arizona Press, 1991, Tables 8.1 and 8.3; open-access PDF, open.uapress.arizona.edu): 'The sampled households in San Mateo Ixtatan have an average of fifty-seven traditional clay vessels. This number is far above the average of other ethnographically documented cases'; Table 8.3 gives cooking-pot use-lives from 0.4 to 13.0 years across the groups compared, 'Pottery having a single function lasts on the order of a few months in my case, and on the order of a few years in Longacre's'. The 4-year life lies inside that range, which is wide; the vessel count and a mass of about a kilogram each give the 5 kg a head. Vessels per household from opened inventories: ten earthen bowls in a 1438 Valencian inventory, six little bowls in 1450, 46 earthen pieces in 1418 (Cambridge, Why did medieval villagers buy earthenware pottery, Valencian countryside 1280-1450, opened, endnotes 55, 56, 58), against 57 in San Mateo Ixtatan; over a household of about five or six people that is two to ten vessels a head, so 5 vessels a head is inside it; the mass is a lower bound on modern bought pots, whose seller specifications (Village Decor, https://villagedecor.in/products/clay-cooking-pot-with-lid-1-5l-to-3-5l, opened) list 1.6 kg for a 1.5 litre lidded clay cooking pot and 2.89 kg for a 3.5 litre one, so a thin-walled hand-made vessel of about a kilogram is the light end (no ethnographic vessel-mass table found), so the stock stays confidence D, a labelled heuristic (Complaints/646). The floor is the stock over its life, as for any durable.
vessels.effectiveness_basis: mass of ware; fired clay and glass are taken equal until a source gives their use-lives separately

writing.floor_basis: No floor: nobody dies or goes cold for want of writing, and a floor is bought whatever it costs, which would put writing into the wage a household must earn. Households spend a share of their surplus on it, and the share applies to the literate part of the population, which is the civilisation's literacy_general, so it grows as schooling spreads.
writing.effectiveness_basis: one written page of a letter or document

money.stock_basis: Silver coin in circulation in a large pre-industrial money economy is of the order of a tenth of a kilogram a head. Source opened (review of Richard Bolton, Money in the Medieval English Economy, quoting Table 2.2, pp. 25-27: https://patricia-saporiti.blogspot.com/2013/06/libros-money-in-medieval-english_9749.html): per capita silver coin in 1310 was 65.5d to 101.3d depending on the population estimate; the early silver penny weighed 1.3 to 1.5 g (Wikipedia, Penny (English coin), https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penny_(English_coin), opened), so 65.5 x 1.3 = 85 g to 101.3 x 1.5 = 152 g a head, midpoint 0.12 kg, rounded to the 0.1 kg held. Wear, loss and hoarding: a numismatic forum estimate (https://forums.collectors.com/discussion/comment/8843720, opened) puts coin loss since 600 BC at about 1 per cent a year with wear about a tenth of that, so a stock life of 1 / 0.01 = 100 years (was 67, no source). Confidence C for the stock (medieval England, not Rome; Duncan-Jones 1994 not opened), D for the life (a forum estimate). The mint's own striking and wear are modelled in sim/economy/mint.py; this entry is only so the labour package sees the engravers and furnacemen that coin replacement keeps at work, and households do not buy it.

light.floor_basis: No floor: nobody dies for want of light after dark, and a floor is bought whatever it costs. Households spend a share of their surplus on it. A tallow candle gives about one candela, about 12.6 lumens, so a thousand lumen-hours is about eighty candle-hours (1000 / 12.566 = 79.6; Wikipedia, Candela, opened: 'A common wax candle has a luminous intensity of roughly 1 cd' and 'a uniform 1 candela source emits 4π lumens (approximately 12.566 lumens)'; that a tallow candle matches a wax one has no source found; confidence D).
light.satiation_basis: TRANSITIONAL heuristic: about four lit evening hours a day at a few hundred lumens a household's room, shared among its people, is the order of what a household lights in a year before more light is waste; not a measured figure. A model of the hours people stay up and the rooms they light would replace it.
light.effectiveness_basis: light given per unit of the good, in thousands of lumen-hours

amusement.floor_basis: No floor: nobody dies for want of a game. Households spend a share of their surplus on it, where a table or a lottery is open to them.
amusement.satiation_basis: TRANSITIONAL heuristic: about four hours of play a week for each person, past which a household's spending on stakes and tables turns to other things; not a measured figure. A model of leisure time would replace it.
amusement.effectiveness_basis: one hour of play at a table, or one numbered chance, taken as equal

household_work.unit: hours of household work done by another
household_work.floor_basis: No market floor: a household does its own cooking, water and fuel, cleaning, grinding and childcare with its own hours first, and hires only what its income lets it (sim/economy/households_work.py). A household hires the hours it would rather sell at the market wage than do itself, up to the work there is, and that is its floor of this need (household_work_year.py); it has no share of surplus spending.
household_work.satiation_basis: The hours a person's share of the household's work takes a year, from data/world/household_work.json (its tasks summed over 365 days; water, fuel and grinding from a Burkina Faso time allocation survey, cooking, cleaning and childcare from Ghana and Sierra Leone time use data, each per adult woman, with the share of adult women a labelled estimate, confidence D); hiring beyond it would be hiring work that is not there. Held equal to that file by a test.
household_work.effectiveness_basis: one hour of a servant's or cook's work

rice_kg.basis: Food energy against wheat: RICE_ENERGY_KCAL_PER_KG over WHEAT_ENERGY_KCAL_PER_KG in sim/world (3600 over 3400). Eaten boiled, not milled.

fat_kg.basis: Not a food here: rendered tallow from sheep and cattle served lighting and soap; the edible animal fat of the period was lard (lard_kg). A good that does serve a need may declare max_share_of_need, the largest share of that need's units it can meet.

lard_kg.basis: Rendered pig fat is nearly pure fat, so a kilogram carries the food energy factor olive_oil_kg carries (2.7 kg wheat equivalent); no source was opened for lard's own energy density.

bread_kg.basis: Calories of the flour in a kilogram of loaf: the flour factor times the flour in a kilogram of bread (data/production/95_bread.json); water and baking add no food energy.

cooked_meal_kg.basis: The food of the ingredients over the mass of the meal, (300 * 1.0 + 200 * 0.1) / 1000 (data/production/95_household_services.json); boiling adds no food energy.

dyed_cloth_kg.basis: Dye adds colour, not cover or warmth, so a kilogram counts as plain cloth does. Labelled placeholder, conf D; retire: Complaints/533 when a need for appearance separates the two.

obsidian_blade_kg.basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC, conf D, no source found for how long a prismatic blade serves before it dulls or breaks. Only a lower bound was read: Hester, Spencer, Busby and Bard, 'Butchering a Deer with Obsidian Tools' (UC Berkeley Archaeological Research Facility, https://digitalassets.lib.berkeley.edu/anthpubs/ucb/proof/pdfs/arf033-04.pdf): a flake "was used for over 30 minutes in cutting tasks, only very minor wear resulted and the tool was still serviceable at the conclusion of the experiment" (38 minutes of use; no end of life reached). A kilogram of blades is about 110 edges that blunt at once, so a kilogram counts far below a kilogram of bronze that serves for years. Edge life, one datum opened: makingflakes.blogspot.com (https://makingflakes.blogspot.com/2013/12/unused-obsidian-knife-hi-all-images.html), one rabbit processed with one obsidian knife left "TOTAL: 47mm of 125mm loss (37.6%)" of the edge, so a knife edge is used up after roughly three small animals. The effectiveness figure itself is still a judgement against a multi-year bronze edge. Retire: Complaint 650.

flint_tool_kg.basis: LABELLED HEURISTIC, conf D, no source found for the service life of a knapped flint tool relative to bronze. Retire: Complaint 650.

fish_kg.basis: Edible fish at 900 kcal a kilogram over wheat grain's 3400 (WHEAT_ENERGY_KCAL_PER_KG); the same energy as the fisher's hours return (data/production/95_fish.json), counted once as the good.

salted_fish_kg.basis: The fresh fish's energy in 700 kg of cured fish from 1000 kg: 0.265 * 1000 / 700; curing adds and loses no energy (data/production/95_fish.json).

garum_kg.basis: A condiment: no food energy is counted, and no need ranks fish sauce among the seasonings yet (seasoning is in pepper equivalents). Bought as an input and traded as a good.

light.basis: Quality against beeswax, the clean-burning reference (factor one): tallow smokes, smells of burnt fat, gutters and sags in summer heat, so a household that can afford wax pays more per unit of light for it. The factor is a household's valuation, not light delivered (lumen-hours stay in effectiveness). Direction read, number not: Wikipedia, Candle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candle, opened) calls tallow cheaper than beeswax, which 'burns cleanly without smoky flame', and tallow gives off an unpleasant smell; no page gave a price or valuation ratio, so 0.7 stays a labelled valuation (Complaint 670).
light.retire: indoor air model (smoke and ventilation), Complaint 670
